analysis.one_liner: Caps US prices of brand-name drugs at the average price charged in six other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since May 2025 with no cosponsors and no action taken on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the federal government to calculate, each year, the average retail list price of every covered prescription drug and biologic in six other wealthy countries: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Drug companies would be barred from charging American patients a list price above that average, and would face a fine equal to ten times the price difference for every unit sold over the limit. Americans currently pay far more than people in comparable countries for many of the same drugs, so the bill targets that gap directly.
analysis.who_benefits: American patients who fill prescriptions for brand-name drugs and biologics, including people on insulin, cancer drugs, and other expensive treatments, would benefit if US list prices were capped at the average of six comparable countries. Employers and taxpayers, who help pay for drugs through insurance premiums and government programs like Medicare, would also share in the savings.

how_it_helps.text: It requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to calculate, each year, the average retail list price of each covered drug in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the UK, and bars the US list price from exceeding that average.

A company that charges more than that average in the US would face a civil penalty equal to ten times the price difference, charged per unit sold, giving manufacturers a strong financial reason to bring US prices in line.
Manufacturers would have to report their US and foreign list prices annually to the government, creating public accountability for international price differences.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost, accepting lower US prices and potentially paying penalties of ten times the price gap on every unit sold above the cap. Their argument is that reduced US revenue could mean less investment in developing new medicines.

drawbacks.text: The penalty is set at ten times the price gap for every unit sold, an unusually severe multiplier; manufacturers would have strong incentive to raise launch prices in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the UK (or delay launching drugs there) to raise the average and soften the US cap.

The bill caps the retail list price, not the net price patients and insurers actually pay after manufacturer rebates and discounts, so companies could offset the cap through the rebate system and patients' out-of-pocket costs might fall less than the headline suggests.
An imposed ceiling on prices for brand-name drugs could reduce the revenue that funds research into new medicines, a cost an honest supporter should acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's promise is substantial: it would directly attack the gap between US and foreign drug prices using a mechanism similar to the Trump administration's 2020 "most favored nation" proposal, which never took effect. But it also has real design problems: an across-the-board price cap pegged to foreign list prices could make some expensive drugs unprofitable, which an honest supporter should acknowledge as a risk of reduced investment or reduced launch of new drugs in the US market; and "retail list price" is not what patients actually pay after rebates and discounts, so the cap could miss the real problem if rebates adjust to compensate. It has no cosponsors and no committee activity, so the bigger obstacle right now is political rather than technical.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in May 2025 and has had no action since, which is where most bills die.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 13, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee that handles drug pricing.
No further action has been taken: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action have been recorded.
Not a single member of the House has signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill without visible support even within its own chamber.

If it did move, the bill would bar US list prices from exceeding the average list price in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the UK, with a penalty of ten times the price gap for each unit sold.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the pharmaceutical industry is better off: as long as the bill sits unaddressed in committee, US list prices remain free to exceed foreign prices. Nothing has been decided yet, and the bill could still move.

for.name: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 13, 2025 and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition has emerged yet.

industries.note: The bill would cap US list prices at the average of six wealthy foreign markets and fine violators ten times the gap per unit, directly cutting into the highest drug prices in the world. Drug makers and their lobby would strongly oppose it.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: Lower list prices could lower the drug costs flowing through insurers and plans, but because the bill targets list prices rather than the rebate system, middlemen's role is untouched. Patients may see only part of the savings.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors and no committee activity, and similar international reference pricing proposals have repeatedly stalled in Congress. Realistically, it will remain unaddressed in committee unless the House leadership decides drug pricing legislation is a priority; the pharmaceutical lobby is among the strongest in Washington, which historically makes moving such a bill an uphill fight.
